verses.translation_literal: I love [him], for YHWH hears my voice, my pleas for favor.
verses.translation_dramatic: I love him. I say it plainly, as one says what has been proved: the LORD hears. He hears my voice, he hears the small broken sound of my asking, and I love him for it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a verb and no object. 'I love' hangs in the air, and only then comes the reason: YHWH hears. Most English versions fill the gap at once (KJV: 'I love the Lord'), and Rashi and Ibn Ezra feel the gap too, reading it as longing ('I long that he hear'); a person who plays this line should start from the bare fact of the love and let the cause arrive a beat later. The love is not a religious formula. It is the love of someone who was heard when no one else was listening.

The tense matters. 'Hears' is an imperfect, a verb of habit: this is not one answered prayer but a pattern the speaker can count on. The second noun, 'tachanunai', is from the root of 'favor', 'grace', so the speaker's own word for the praying is 'my asking for favor', what a person with no claim says to someone with all the power. KJV's 'supplications' is right but Latinate and cold; the Hebrew word is the one a beggar uses. It is a plural, and BBE's 'my prayer' flattens it.

philological_notes.note: The verb has no stated object. In the Bible love is mostly said of persons; the commentators supply 'the LORD' or read the line as a longing. The Hebrew keeps the reader waiting for the 'because'.
'Pleas for favor', from the root of 'grace' (chen). It is the word of one who has no claim, and it echoes the 'chanun' ('gracious') of v.5.

verses.translation_literal: For he has inclined his ear to me, and in my days I will call out.
verses.translation_dramatic: He leaned in. The LORD bent his ear down toward me, as one bends to catch a whisper, and so for as many days as I am given, I will call.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Inclined his ear' is the physical picture behind the abstraction: God bends down toward the speaker, the way an adult bends to a child or to a sick man whose voice is thin. KJV makes this a neat argument ('therefore will I call upon him as long as I live'), and the 'therefore' and 'as long as I live' are both the translator's: the Hebrew has only 'and in my days I will call'. The literal 'in my days' is a Hebrew way of saying 'my whole lifetime', but it also keeps a human scale, the daily cry of a life, not a single rescue.

Because 'ki' ('for') opens both v.1 and v.2, the two verses chain: I love him / because he hears / because he leaned. The actor should let each 'because' push the speech forward. Rashi hears a division of the days: the days of distress for calling, the days of rescue for praise.

philological_notes.note: 'He inclined his ear' is an idiom for attentive listening. The verb means 'stretch out, bend', so the picture is of God bending down. It is the opposite of the idols' ears that do not hear (Ps 115:6, the psalm just before).
'In my days': KJV's 'as long as I live' is an interpretation. Meiri reads it as 'not once only but in all my moments', Metzudat David as 'on every day I call'.

verses.translation_literal: They surrounded me, the cords of death, and the straits of Sheol found me; trouble and sorrow I find.
verses.translation_dramatic: The ropes of death closed around me. The narrow places of Sheol came searching, and they found me; and I, too, went on finding, everywhere I turned, only trouble and sorrow.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the picture that gives the psalm its fear: a hunter's cord, drawn around a man until he cannot move, and the narrow places of the underworld looking for him. 'Chevel' means rope, but also the pangs of childbirth; Radak and Metzudat Zion both take the plural in that second sense, 'pains', which is why KJV has 'sorrows of death' and 'pains of hell'. The two readings are not rivals: a cord that tightens like labor. Rashi prefers a third, 'bands' of enemies. The actor can choose; the Hebrew deliberately keeps all three.

KJV's 'hell' for Sheol is the most misleading word in the verse. Sheol is not a place of fire and judgment but the shadowed home of all the dead, a pit at the edge of the world, and 'metzarei' plays on 'tzarah', 'trouble' two words later: the straits (tzar) of Sheol find a man in a strait (tzarah). The last verb turns the tables: they found me, and I find; the verb 'find' occurs twice, once with the hunters as subject and once with the speaker, as if the man runs into the trouble he flees.

philological_notes.note: 'Cords of death', also 'pangs'. The same phrase appears in Ps 18:5 (Hebrew 18:5-6). The root has two meanings, rope and the pains of labor, and both are heard here.
'The straits of Sheol'. It sounds like 'tzarah' ('trouble') in the same verse. Rashi glosses it 'the borders of Sheol'; Radak says the second clause only doubles the first in other words.
'I find', the same verb as 'they found me'. Radak points out that misfortune finds a man but a man also walks to meet it, not knowing his hour.

verses.translation_literal: And on the name of YHWH I call out: 'I beg you, YHWH, rescue my life!'
verses.translation_dramatic: And I called on the name of the LORD, and I said it: 'Please, LORD, I beg you; save my life.'
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb 'I call out' is the same one as in v.2 ('in my days I will call out'); here it is given content, the exact words. The line moves from description to speech, from a man telling us about his prayer to the prayer itself, and the actor should drop the voice from narration to naked address. KJV's 'Then called I' adds a 'then' that the Hebrew lacks, turning a habit into a single episode.

'Anah' is a particle of pleading, spelled with a final he here instead of the usual alef; Radak notes that it is one of the places where the spelling differs from the reading and says the stress falls on the first syllable because of the long vowel. It is a short, urgent word, more 'please, I beg' than KJV's polite 'I beseech thee'. 'Naphshi' is 'my nefesh', which can mean soul but first means throat, breath, the living self: what the speaker asks is not that his soul go to heaven but that his breath be saved.

philological_notes.note: An interjection of pleading, written with he here for the usual alef. Radak says the stress is on the first syllable; Metzudat Zion says the he stands in place of the alef.
'My life, my breath, myself'. KJV's 'my soul' makes the request sound otherworldly; the verb 'malet' is used of fleeing to safety, an escape from physical danger.

verses.translation_literal: Gracious [is] YHWH, and righteous, and our God [is] compassionate.
verses.translation_dramatic: Gracious is the LORD, and just. Our God, our own God, is full of compassion.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the cry of v.4 comes a creed, said in the first person plural: 'our God'. The singer who stood alone in the straits now steps back into the congregation. This is the language of Exodus 34:6, where God proclaims himself 'compassionate and gracious' (the two words 'rachum' and 'chanun'), and the psalm here turns a famous formula into something a person can say to himself. The three adjectives, 'chanun', 'tzaddik', 'merachem', are in a line that moves from grace (what he gives freely) through justice (what he keeps faithful) to mother-love: 'rechem' is the womb, and 'merachem' means to be moved as from the womb.

KJV's 'yea' is an addition. The Hebrew makes the sentence a plain chain of 'and': grace, justice, motherly pity. Malbim reads the three as three reasons God hears: because he gives for nothing, because he repays the righteous, and because he pities the poor. An actor can take any of them; the point is that the speaker does not argue from his merit.

philological_notes.note: 'Gracious', the one who gives favor unearned. It picks up the 'tachanunai' of v.1 (my pleas for favor): the plea and the answer share a root.
'Is compassionate', a participle. Ibn Ezra takes it as equal to 'rachum'. The root is that of 'rechem', womb: the feeling of a mother for the child of her body.

verses.translation_literal: Guarding the simple [is] YHWH; I was low, and me he saved.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD keeps watch over the simple. I had been brought low; and it was me, me, that he lifted out.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Peta'im', the 'simple', are not fools in our sense but the unguarded, the naive, those who have no cunning and no wall: in Proverbs they are the young men who can be talked into anything. Radak's comment is the best: the simple man knows no trick for escaping his trouble, so God keeps him, and even the wise man cannot rely on his schemes. KJV's 'preserveth' is fine; 'simple' needs to be played as a vulnerable innocence, not stupidity, which is why the speaker immediately includes himself.

The syntax puts the pronoun forward: 'and to me he saved', with the 'to me' ahead of the verb and more emphatic than KJV's flat 'he helped me'. After the tight cluster of general truths (v.5), the line returns to the individual: this is not a doctrine, this is what happened to me. 'Daloti' echoes 'dal', the poor, the thin, the low: 'I was drawn thin'. KJV's 'helped' for 'hoshia' loses the root of 'salvation' (yesha), the same word as Joshua's name.

philological_notes.note: 'The simple, the naive'. Radak and Meiri read it as those who have no scheme to save themselves. In Proverbs the 'peti' is the unformed, the easily led.
'I was low, I hung thin'. The root gives 'dal', the weak and poor. Radak notes the stress falls on the last syllable, marking the perfect.
'He saved': the hiphil of the root of 'salvation'; the same root gives the name Joshua/Jesus.

verses.translation_literal: Return, my soul, to your resting places, for YHWH has dealt bountifully upon you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come back, my soul. Come home to your resting places; the LORD has been good to you, and the long fear is over.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker talks to his own 'nefesh', his breath, his self, as to a person who has gone astray in terror, and tells it to come home. This is a man coaching himself out of panic, and an actor should not pitch the line as a hymn but as a tender, firm second-person command, as one calls back a frightened child from the street. Radak imagines the self-address belonging to the time of the trouble itself: even then he said, 'return to your rest, to God, for he will be your rest.'

The plural 'menuchayekhi', 'your resting places', is a plural of fullness: not one bed but every kind of safe stopping place. KJV's 'rest' flattens it. The long endings 'ayekhi' (on the verbs and prepositions that carry 'you', feminine) are an old, archaic form of 'you', which Metzudat Zion notes as a surplus yod; the feminine 'you' is grammatical, because nefesh is a feminine noun, and keeps the tenderness: the speaker addresses 'her'. 'Gamal', 'dealt bountifully', is a word for repaying, for good or ill. Meiri notes that without a measure of requital it means a first kindness.

philological_notes.note: 'To your resting places': a plural and an archaic feminine ending. The yod is a surplus, as Metzudat Zion says. The soul is addressed as a woman because nefesh is feminine.
'He dealt with, repaid'; used for good or for ill. Meiri says that without a measure of requital the word is used for kindness freely begun, and cites Ps 13:6.

verses.translation_literal: For you have rescued my life from death, my eye from tears, my foot from stumbling.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you drew me out of death. You kept my eyes from the weeping and my feet from the fall.
verses.directors_commentary:
The singer turns from himself to God and says 'you'. Everything up to now was told about the LORD; now the LORD is in the room. The shift is the emotional hinge of the first half of the psalm, and the director should mark it: the actor lifts his eyes, no longer at his own soul but at the One who did it.

The three things rescued, life, eye and foot, are a short inventory of the body: the whole person from death, the face from tears, the feet from stumbling. 'Chilatzta', 'you rescued', is the verb of pulling out or drawing off, as one pulls a sandal or a sword from its sheath; Metzudat Zion links it to 'In trouble you called and I drew you out' (Ps 81:8). KJV's 'delivered' is acceptable but has no pulling in it. The last word 'dechi' is a stumble that throws a man down, a push (the root of 'push, thrust'); Radak reads it also as the pushing of exile. The parallel 'rescue from' repeated three times (with the 'min' prefix on each) gives a drumbeat that the actor should keep.

philological_notes.note: 'You drew out, rescued'. The root means to pull out or draw off, as in 'strip off a sandal'. Metzudat Zion links it to Ps 81:8: 'in trouble you called and I rescued you.'
'A push, a fall'. KJV 'falling' is right; Radak reads it as being driven away, as in exile.

verses.translation_literal: I will walk about before YHWH in the lands of the living.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will walk in the presence of the LORD, here, in the country of the living.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is the reflexive 'hithalech', a walk back and forth, a daily going about: not a march but life's ordinary pacing, now done 'before the LORD', in his sight and presence. The prayer ends in the plainest of promises, to go on walking. 'Before YHWH' is a phrase for service and for living in his presence, and the scene is no temple, only the ground.

'Artzot', 'lands', is plural. KJV, ASV and BBE all say 'land of the living', but the Hebrew has the plural 'lands of the living', and the plural is odd enough to ask what it means. Rashi thinks it is the Land of Israel, from which the speaker was driven by Saul; Ibn Ezra, reading from the feet in the previous verse, says it is the face of the earth as against the ground under it; Meiri allows either this world or the world to come. In any case the idea is a country defined by being alive, the opposite of Sheol in v.3.

philological_notes.note: The reflexive stem: 'I will walk about, go to and fro', a continuing habit, not a single march. This is the verb used of Enoch and Noah walking with God.
'In the lands of the living', a plural. Rashi: the Land of Israel; Ibn Ezra: on the earth's surface, not beneath it; Meiri: this world or the world to come.

verses.translation_literal: I believed, when I would speak: I, I was afflicted greatly.
verses.translation_dramatic: I held on to my faith even when I spoke the words: 'I have been broken, utterly broken.'
verses.directors_commentary:
This is one of the most argued lines in the Psalter, and the director should not pretend otherwise. 'Ki' can mean 'for, because, when, that, even though'; the verb 'adaber' is a bare 'I will speak' with no object. KJV and Webster say 'I believed, therefore have I spoken', which is the version Paul quotes (2 Corinthians 4:13) from the Greek, where the psalm is Psalm 115; the Hebrew does not quite say 'therefore'. Meiri reads 'I believed even in the things I said to my own heart'; Radak reads 'my faith was great, for I spoke even while you afflicted me'; BBE prefers 'I still had faith, though I said'. The Hebrew keeps the choice open, and the translation should too: 'I believed, when I would speak'.

The second half is clear. 'Ani aniti me'od', 'I, I was afflicted greatly', puts the pronoun forward, stressing the 'I', and uses the verb 'ana', 'to be bowed down', whose adjective 'ani' is the 'poor, humbled' man of the Psalms. The 'I' is abrupt and almost bitter: what I said I said as a man who had been brought as low as a man can go. The sound of 'aniti' and 'ani' next to each other, 'I, afflicted', makes a stammer the actor can use. KJV's colon after 'greatly afflicted' is an addition: in the Hebrew the sentence simply stops and the next verse supplies what he said.

philological_notes.note: Four readings: 'I believed, therefore I speak' (the Septuagint, and KJV), 'I believed even when I spoke', 'I believed when I would speak', 'I believe when I speak' (Ibn Ezra). 'Ki' leaves all of them open. Radak and Metzudat David take the faith to be the point, with the speaking as the time of affliction.
'I was afflicted, bowed down'. The root is the source of 'ani', the 'poor and humbled one' of the Psalms. The Targum has a different sense, 'I praised greatly', reading the verb as answer or sing.

verses.translation_literal: I, I said in my haste: every human [is] a liar.
verses.translation_dramatic: I said it in my panic, running: 'Every man is a liar.'
verses.directors_commentary:
'Chafaz' is the word for hurry, alarm, the flight of a person who is running and cannot think: it is used of David hurrying away from Saul in 1 Samuel 23:26, which Rashi connects to this verse, and Metzudat David too ('when I was hurrying to flee from Saul'). The speaker confesses what he said at his worst and does not defend it. 'In my haste' is a time-stamp: the words belong to the moment of terror, not to the man he is now. BBE's 'in my fear' is an interpretation, but a fair one.

The pronoun 'ani' is again put forward ('I, I said'), echoing 'ani aniti' in v.10: I, afflicted; I, who said. The man owns both. 'Kol ha'adam', 'every adam', is all humankind, not 'all men' (KJV) in the sense of males, and 'kozev', 'a liar', is a participle: a man is a deceiver, a thing that fails, as a stream that dries (Rashi cites Isa 58:11, 'whose waters do not fail'). So the despair is not about morals but about trust: no human is a water you can drink. Rashi reads it with Absalom's betrayal; Radak, as faith in the promise of the throne against anyone who said David would not reign. Both are readings from stories, not from the verse itself.

philological_notes.note: 'In my haste, alarm': a flight in fear. It is the root used in 1 Sam 23:26 ('David was hurrying to get away from Saul'), which Rashi and Metzudat David connect here.
'A liar, one who fails'. Rashi says the root means a lack of the thing relied upon, and cites Isa 58:11, a spring whose waters do not 'fail' (yekhazzevu).

verses.translation_literal: What shall I return to YHWH, all his benefits upon me?
verses.translation_dramatic: What can I give back to the LORD? So much he has done for me, all of it laid on me; what is there to answer it with?
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has gone from the pit to the question every rescued person asks: how do you repay what cannot be repaid? The verb 'ashiv', 'shall I return', is the same root as 'shuvi' in v.7 ('return, my soul'): the soul was told to come back, and now the man asks what he can bring back. The sense is of a debt, but a debt that can't be met: Radak says it plainly, that there was no merit in him and the whole thing was favor.

The unusual word is 'tagmulohi'. The ending -ohi is Aramaic-looking, standing for Hebrew -av ('his'): Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion each say so, and compare 'alohi' for 'alav'. It is the only appearance of the noun 'tagmul' in the Bible, and it is built on 'gamal' of v.7: the LORD 'dealt bountifully' (gamal), and the man asks what to do with all the 'dealings' (tagmulim). KJV's 'benefits' does catch the sense of good done, and the 'toward me' is right, but the Hebrew's 'upon me' keeps a weight: they lie on him like a load. The verse that follows brings the only answer he has, a cup, a name and a vow.

philological_notes.note: 'His benefits': the only occurrence of the noun. The ending -ohi is Aramaic-looking for -av, 'his'. Ibn Ezra, however, thinks it is two words, 'tagmulo' and 'hi'. The noun is built on 'gamal' (v.7).
'Shall I return, repay'. It is the root of 'shuvi' (v.7): the soul was bidden to return, and now the man asks what to return.

verses.translation_literal: A cup of salvations I will lift up, and on the name of YHWH I will call.
verses.translation_dramatic: The cup of deliverance — I will raise it high, and over it, aloud, I will say the Name of the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has just asked, "What shall I return to the LORD?" (v. 12), and the answer is not a payment but a gesture: he lifts a cup. Play it slowly, with the cup actually raised. Whether this is a wine libation poured at a thanksgiving meal, as Rashi and Radak think (the Levites sing over wine, says Rashi), or the 'cup' as one's allotted portion, as in Ps 16:5 (the view Ibn Ezra attributes to Moses ibn Gikatilla), the effect is the same: he answers God's giving by receiving again, in public, with thanks.

The KJV's "take" is fair for nasa but flattens the physical verb 'lift', and it turns the plural 'salvations' into a single abstract 'salvation'; the plural suggests many rescues, or rescue in full measure. The KJV also turns 'on the name I will call' into 'call upon', which is correct but hides that the same phrase returns in v. 17, forming a refrain. Note that 'calling on the name' was the cry for help of v. 4; now the same act becomes praise. The distress cry and the thanksgiving cry are one phrase.

philological_notes.note: 'Cup of salvations'. The plural of yeshuah is intensive or abstract. Medieval commentators split on whether the cup is a literal drink of thanksgiving or a portion in life, as in 'the LORD is my allotted portion and my cup' (Ps 16:5).
'I will lift up'. Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'raise' (aRim), from great joy. The ordinary verb for lifting a cup, the hands, or the voice.

verses.translation_literal: My vows to YHWH I will pay, in front of — please — all his people.
verses.translation_dramatic: What I promised the LORD in the dark hour, I will pay now: before all his people, where every eye can see it.
verses.directors_commentary:
Vows were made in trouble: 'if you save me, I will give...' (see Jonah 2:9, Ps 66:13-14). Once the rescue came, the debt was real, and ancient law took it seriously (Deut 23:22-24). But he does not pay quietly. The sting is in 'before all his people': a vow is paid at the sanctuary in the presence of the community, and the payment doubles as testimony. A thank-offering meal was shared, so his rescue becomes their feast.

The KJV's 'now in the presence of' is accurate; its 'now' translates the small particle na. Commentators argue over whether na attaches to 'I will pay' (Radak, Meiri: 'I will pay now') or to 'before' (YLT 'I pray you'). The particle is softly urgent, as if he cannot wait. The odd ending on negdah ('before') is likely a directional he; Radak and Meiri think it is a stray extra letter. Play the word as a small catch in the voice.

philological_notes.note: 'In front of, please'. The ending -ah on negdah is either a directional he or an extra letter; na is an urging particle, attached by Radak to 'I will pay' ('now').

verses.translation_literal: Costly in the eyes of YHWH [is] the death to his faithful ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: Heavy in the LORD's eyes, a costly thing, is death when it comes for those who are faithful to him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is calm, but it is not a comfort for every reader. The KJV's 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints' sounds like a funeral greeting: death as a prize, the saint's end as something the LORD treasures. The Hebrew יָקָר is wider than 'precious'. It means valuable, costly, heavy, hard to give up. Rashi hears it as 'a hard and heavy matter in his eyes, to put his faithful ones to death'. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion compare Ps 49:9 ("the redemption of their life is costly"), and Radak compares "their blood was costly in his eyes" (Ps 72:14). So the speaker has just come back from the edge and says that the LORD does not spend the lives of his people cheaply. Play it as the reason he is alive to speak, not as a verdict on death.

'Saints' is the second softening. חֲסִידָיו are those who keep hesed, covenant loyalty, to him: his faithful, his loyal ones. The word has no halo. In a world where a master's household and property counted for his honour and a client's death shamed his patron, the line also carries a plain claim about the LORD's stake in his people. The odd ending of הַמָּוְתָה ("death-ward", with the directional ה) has the sense of death arriving at them. Ibn Ezra reads that ה as an ending that does not mark the feminine, like שְׁאוֹלָה.

philological_notes.note: Valuable, but also costly or heavy. The classical commentators read it here as 'hard, grave' in the LORD's sight, as in Ps 49:9, so the verse says that the death of the faithful is not to be spent lightly. 'Precious' alone loses the weight.
'His faithful ones', the people who keep hesed (loyalty) to him. The KJV's 'saints' adds a later church sense. The Hebrew describes loyalty, not holiness of life.
'The death' with an added ה. Rashi compares הַבַּיְתָה, 'homeward', so it may point toward the faithful; Ibn Ezra says the ה is only an ending, like שְׁאוֹלָה, and not a feminine marker.

verses.translation_literal: Ah, YHWH! For I am your servant; I am your servant, the son of your maidservant. You have loosened my fetters.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD — yes, I am yours. Your servant, your servant, born in your house of your own handmaid. And you have undone the bonds that held me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone drops to its most personal. Anah is an interjection, 'ah, I beg you', sounding both like a plea and like thanks; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion note it can mean either (as in Exod 32:31). The repetition, 'I am your servant, I am your servant', is the hinge of the psalm: deliverance is credited not to merit but to belonging.

'Son of your maidservant' is the key phrase. A slave born in the household (yelid bayit) was more secure than one bought in the market: raised inside, owned from birth, with a claim on the master's care. Rashi and Meiri say precisely this: he is no market purchase, but one raised in the house. Moderns miss that it is a plea, not a self-lowering. The KJV renders 'thy handmaid' with the same archaism and keeps 'bonds' for moserai, losing the physical image: moserim are cords, or yoke-straps, as in Job 39:5. The verb pittachta, 'you have opened', is the word for opening a knot or a lock; the KJV's 'loosed' is acceptable. The picture is of a prisoner, or an animal, whose ropes are untied.

philological_notes.note: 'Son of your maidservant': a household-born slave, whose standing is firmer than that of a slave bought from the market. Rashi and Meiri read it as a claim of closeness; the same phrase appears in Ps 86:16.

'You have loosened my fetters'. The lamed before moserai is, according to Ibn Ezra, an extra lamed (like 'they killed Abner', harGu leAvner); Metzudat Zion glosses moserot as the straps of captivity, citing Job 39:5.

verses.translation_literal: To you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and on the name of YHWH I will call.
verses.translation_dramatic: To you I will bring the offering of thanks; and the Name of the LORD, I will call it out.
verses.directors_commentary:
Verse 13 returns, with the cup now matched by the animal. The todah, 'thanksgiving offering', was a peace-offering (Lev 7:11-15) and must be eaten the same day, so a whole table of guests had to be invited; Radak understands the line this way, 'I will call the many to be with me at the sacrifice, and they will hear my thanks'. This is why it ends with a public call.

The Hebrew gives a pun that English can echo: 'I will sacrifice a sacrifice' (ezbach zevach), the verb and its noun together. The KJV's 'I will offer ... the sacrifice of thanksgiving' hides the play and the verb zavach, 'slaughter for a meal'. Also, 'to you' is placed first, a word of address, where English puts it last. After the shared prayer in vv. 13-14, here God is spoken to directly again.

philological_notes.note: A cognate accusative: 'I will sacrifice a sacrifice'. The todah was a communal meal, which explains the public setting of v. 18.
'Thanksgiving, confession, praise'. The root yadah means both 'to thank' and 'to acknowledge publicly', which is why the sacrifice is spoken as well as offered.

verses.translation_literal: My vows to YHWH I will pay, before all his people, please.
verses.translation_dramatic: My vows to the LORD I will pay, and here, now, in front of his whole people, let it be done.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse repeats v. 14 almost word for word, and the two are a refrain. The first time the vow is a promise made in the dark; here it is a promise about to be kept in public. Ibn Ezra and Radak both ask why the line is said twice. Ibn Ezra says it names the place: the vow can be paid only at the LORD's house, which is why the next verse names its courts. A thanksgiving sacrifice (v. 17) was eaten at a shared meal, so 'before all his people' is not a flourish: the worshippers are the audience, and the man's rescue has to be witnessed.

The small word נָּא is the one that the KJV turns into 'now'. It is a particle of urging, 'please, I beg', and the word order places it after נֶגְדָה ("in front of", with a directional ה, 'into the presence of'). It is a request or resolve to be allowed, not just a time marker, and YLT's 'let me complete, I pray you' sees it. The speaker is asking for the chance to be seen paying. Radak and Meiri place the payment in the courts in Jerusalem. Meiri also notes that some books end the psalm here and count 'Praise the LORD, all nations' (Ps 117:1-2) as a separate psalm, while in his books those two verses close Ps 116. The numbering used here, like the Masoretic text's, keeps them as Ps 117.

philological_notes.note: 'In front of, in the presence of', with a directional ה, then נָא, 'please'. The particle makes it an urgent wish. The KJV's 'now' turns it into time.
'My vows', glossed by Rashi as 'the sacrifices that I vowed'. The same phrase appears in v. 14, and Ibn Ezra says the repetition names the place where it is paid, the LORD's house.

verses.translation_literal: In the courts of the house of YHWH, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: In the courts of the LORD's house, in the heart of you, Jerusalem. Praise the LORD — Hallelujah!
verses.directors_commentary:
The place is finally named, and the camera widens from one man with a cup to a whole city. The speaker turns and speaks to Jerusalem itself, 'in your midst', as if the walls and the crowd were listening. Then the closing call is Hallelu-Yah, the plural command 'praise!' addressed to everyone present. Radak hears it as the speaker calling all the crowd to join him.

The 'courts' (chatzerot) are the open enclosures around the sanctuary, where lay worshippers could stand and where thank-offerings were eaten; the sanctuary itself was not entered. The KJV smooths 'in your midst' into 'in the midst of thee', fine, but also hides the archaic feminine suffix in betokheki, which has a final yod: Radak and Ibn Ezra call it extra, a poetic fullness, as in other forms like 'your sicknesses' (tachaluayki) in the Hebrew. The KJV 'Praise ye the Lord' loses the divine short name Yah, which sounds as a single breath. Play the last word as a shout.

philological_notes.note: 'In your midst', with the poetic feminine suffix -ekhi; Rashi says it equals betokhekh, and Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion say the yod is extra.
'Praise Yah': a plural imperative, 'all of you praise', with the short form of the divine name. Radak: 'all of you praise Yah, my people'.
